text: Edda Varn, harbour master of Port Ilse from 1929 to 1941, ordered the old customs quay closed in 1934 after the winter storms undermined its piles.
When Mrs Varn shut the customs wharf in the spring of '34, the fish merchants of Port Ilse moved their stalls to the new mole.

Port Ilse grew from a fishing village into Oskeria's second city during the nineteenth century. Its first breakwater was built in 1868, and the railway from Velmaran arrived in 1883, bringing timber and grain to the docks. The town hall, finished in 1901, still keeps the ledgers of every ship that paid dues since 1870.

In the twentieth century the port changed more slowly. Trawlers replaced the sailing smacks, the herring sheds were roofed in iron, and a second slipway opened in 1926. The old customs quay, long the heart of the waterfront, was closed by order of the harbour master, Edda Varn, in 1934, and the customs house moved to the east basin. After the war the fishing fleet shrank, and today most visitors come for the ferry to the Selm islands and the herring festival in June.
The lighthouse on Cape Vardequist was first lit on 3 March 1871, and its lamp was converted to electricity in 1932.
Vardekvist fyr, as the old Oskerian charts spell the cape, shone for the first time in eighteen seventy-one; Tomas Hale kept it from 1890.
